newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Normality, Albanian style, after anarchy subsides.
newsitem.headline: Normality, Albanian style, after anarchy subsides.

text.p: Albanian troops guarding Tirana airport as part of efforts to restore order after weeks of armed mayhem now feel relaxed enough to enjoy a drink or a few frames of pool between stints on their armoured vehicles.

As soldiers and police armed with Kalashnikov assault rifles patrol the airfield and mount guard on the roof of the terminal building, the crackling public address system announces calmly: "The flight to Sofia is now ready for boarding."

The airport only reopened to passenger and cargo traffic on Thursday after a week-long shutdown forced when Albania's recent outbreak of anarchy peaked. Those boarding the resumed flights exude relief at being able to get out of the country.

Despite the tension, the airport seems to have been effectively secured, allowing the soldiers to take a break in a nearby cafe, even offering reporters a drink, and in a small concrete shed housing a pair of pool tables.
Albania is returning to some form of normality, but it is a peculiarly Albanian normality.
In the capital Tirana, a curfew is still in force and a nightly patrol up and down the main boulevard by a convoy of tanks, armoured vehicles and vans full of armed police has become a commonplace.
In one of the main hotels where the international press corps is headquartered, only particularly heavy bursts of evening firing cause the restaurant waiters to kill the lights and draw the blinds.

At this point the journalists feel obliged to interrupt dinner to investigate. But, with the curfew on, they can usually only manage to peer out the windows and speculate. The best way to do this is with a glass of wine in hand.
The hotel lifts carry a notice saying: "Do not use the elevator in case of fire."
"I wonder if that includes automatic weapons fire," one British reporter wondered aloud.
Away from the hotel, residents of the capital say that, while the random firing of looted weapons into the air has diminished in recent days, it remains a distinct hazard in some areas.

Blerta, a 21-year-old English language student, said that a man living on the third floor of her apartment block insisted on firing his looted Kalashnikov out the window. "This is a problem for us because we live on the sixth floor," she said.
With the streets still littered with used ammunition, conversations are best carried out under an overhanging roof as protection from rounds fired skywards and returning randomly to earth.

Accidental shootings have accounted for most of the more than 100 deaths since angry citizens reacted to the loss of their savings in shady pyramid investment schemes by looting thousands of weapons from army barracks.
While the south of the country remains in the hands of rebels who began the uprising in January, government efforts to restore order are apparent in the north.

In the northern regional capital of Shkoder, the call to prayer from the minaret of the central mosque is followed immediately by a relay of the afternoon news from Radio Tirana, which draws a small audience in the town square.

In his office, the local prefect, Elham Sharra, interrupts his thoughts on how he is trying to repair the effects of two nights of looting and burning to remark that the last time he was in Britain he paid a visit to Liverpool's Cavern Club, home of the Beatles.
